items.title: 67251_Chuck Green oral history interview
items.q: I think he was unknown up here at that time. He used to travel on the TOBA... It was kind of popular then, dancing, especially tap dancing. That was on account of Jack Wiggins...

ctx.x: Do you think he had the greatest influence?

Yes. Definitely. Yeah, he had the greatest influence, he and John Bubbles, you see, of Buck and Bubbles. See, because Jack Wiggins was not -- I think he was unknown up here at that time. He used to travel on the TOBA, and that was mostly in the south, you know. And therefore, Bill Bojangles Robinson was making tap dancing recognizable when people would -- when they'd speak of tap dancing, they'd speak of it like they speak of ballet, you see. Because there was a lot of different works in tap dancing, see? You had…

dancing. They had novelty tap dancing, you see. And they had trick tap dancing. His tap dancing consisted of steps. And that was tap dancing. Because he would always say -- he had a routine where he would say, "Number one tap step." And when he would demonstrate the number one tap step. But it was fascinating. As I say, they all would do some kind of buck. See? And he had a way of doing the time step, and he called that number one step, you see?
